Abstract
Heterogeneous and multi-device nodes are increasingly com-
mon in high-performance computing and data centers, yet
existing programming models often lack simple, transparent,
and portable support for these diverse architectures. The
main contribution of this work is the development of novel
SEER capabilities to address this challenge by providing a
descriptive programming model that allows applications to
seamlessly leverage heterogeneous nodes across various de-
vice types. SEER uses efficient memory management and can
select the proper device[s] depending on the computational
cost of the applications. This is completely transparent to
the programmer, thereby providing a highly productive pro-
gramming environment. Integrating extreme heterogeneity
into the SEER library as shown with the use of NVIDIA and
AMD GPUs simultaneously allows it to expand and exploit
the performance possibilities. Our analysis based on the well-
known Conjugate Gradient algorithm reports accelerations
above 1.5× on computationally demanding steps of such an
algorithm by using both architectures simultaneously.

SEER
As computational loads increase and Moore’s law approaches
its limits, supercomputers face growing energy demands.
One possible approach to this issue is to leverage extreme het-
erogeneity. New techniques can be developed to efficiently
maximize the utilization of diverse hardware as shown on
SEER [Valero-Lara and Vetter 2023b]. SEER is a C++ library
that provides a descriptive programming model to enable
applications to benefit from heterogeneous nodes in a trans-
parent and portable way across multiple device types. SEER is
composed of two main modules: memory and compute (par-
allel constructs). Both modules have different and separate
implementations depending on the back end. The back ends
are OpenMP, CUDA, HIP, and OpenMP Target as they are
the most relevant parallel programming models used in cur-
rent and upcoming HPC architectures (e.g., multicore CPUs
and NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs). SEER differs from other
existing data-parallel C++ solutions, such as Kokkos [Trott
et al. 2021; Valero-Lara et al. 2024, 2022; Valero-Lara and Vet-
ter 2023a], RAJA [Beckingsale et al. 2019] and SYCL [Reyes
et al. 2020] models in different ways: (1) Instead of the pro-
grammer specifying which device to use at compilation time,
SEER decides in a transparent way which devices (i.e., back
ends) to use at run time. (2) The devices to be used can
change along the execution of the application depending
on the computational cost of the operations carried out and
the hardware characteristics. (3) Different devices and/or
back ends can coexist and be used simultaneously, thereby
providing a real heterogeneous and multi-device solution.
(4) The computation is defined as functions. These functions
are written in C++ and are compatible with all back ends.
In SEER the memory management (see Figure 1) is com-
pletely transparent to the programmer. The programmer
does not have to know which device’s memory (memory
space) is being used or if necessary memory transfers be-
tween CPU and GPUs or between GPUs are conducted, this
is all taken care of without their intervention. The memory
spaces of the different devices are managed dynamically ac-
cording to the decisions taken by the SEER library, which
depends on the features of the hardware and connectivity,
and the computational cost of the applications (autotuning).

Extending SEER-node for Extreme
Heterogeneity
The SEER-node (see Figure 4) enables SEER to use multi-
ple devices concurrently, improving performance without
adding code complexity. It achieves this by using two macros,
SEER_FORK(N) and SEER_JOIN, to express parallelism. The
macro SEER_FORK(N) defines the parallel degree to be ex-
ploited. This work extends SEER-node’s capabilities (see Fig-
ure 3) to run in parallel independent data-parallel constructs
encapsulated into SEER_FORK(N) and SEER_JOIN primitives
on different devices.
Figure 3. SEER-node diagram.
There are various challenges to implementing extreme
heterogeneity, such as data dependencies, launch overheads,
and the coordination of multiple accelerators. Each device
has its own compiler, which allows it to optimally use its
device using various flags, macros, functions, etc. To keep
each devices’ capabilities, the compiler flags were specified
for each device. Compiling and linking each file and library
was required to ensure each device functioned optimally to
meet the requirements on data dependencies, and reduce
launch overheads when executing with extreme heterogene-
ity. To ensure the coordination of each device, the library
for each respective GPU was added to the executable. Each
parallel execution used an identifier (last parameter of par-
allel_for[_reduce]_node) to split the computational load for
either the AMD GPU or NVIDIA GPU.
To enable SEER for extreme heterogeneity, SEER-node
macros were re-implemented to ensure that independent
SEER parallel constructs can be deployed on different GPU
architectures. Following the original implementation, we
use OpenMP as the orchestrator to make the deployment in
parallel.
The test case used is the Conjugate Gradient (CG) algo-
rithm as its characteristics represent real scenarios. CG is an
iterative method for solving sparse linear equations, used
in various fields: finite element methods, partial differen-
tial equations, and structural analysis. CG can benefit from
parallelization [Catalán et al. 2019], particularly in its most
time-consuming steps. While some parts of the algorithm
have data dependencies limiting parallelism, operations like
DOT, which performs a dot product between two vectors,
and AXPY, which performs a scalar-vector product and adds
the result to a vector, can be computed in parallel on differ-
ent devices. With a high computational load, CG becomes
a good test case to measure the performance and efficiency
of the extreme heterogeneous systems. These computations
usually take more than half of the execution time of the
entire CG computation. This test case pushes forward the

Performance Evaluation
We used ORNL’s Experimental Computing Lab (ExCL) <https:
//www.excl.ornl.gov/> for the performance evaluation. ExCL
is a laboratory for computer science research that offers het-
erogeneous resources and full configuration of the software
stack. Through ExCL, we access the Zenith system. Zenith
is a heterogeneous system composed of AMD and NVIDIA
GPUs. It is equipped with one AMD Threadripper 3970X
CPU, one NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU, and one AMD
Radeon RX 6900 GPU. Our test case was compiled using the
nvcc compiler (V12.3.103) for the NVIDIA GPU and the hipcc
compiler (6.0) for the AMD GPU. The linkage of HIP and
CUDA libraries was done via the AMD clang g++ (17.0.0)
compiler. The test cases use single-precision.
Figure 5. SEER-node performance for AXPY (left) and DOT
(right) computations as part of the CG algorithm on ORNL’s
ExCL Zenith system.
The same code was used for both cases (AMD+NVIDIA
and AMD in Figure 5). As discussed previously, our focus is
on computational load for the GPUs which represent more
than 90% of the total GFLOPs provided in the systems tested
and assist with energy efficiency. In this case, the CPU is
primarily used for orchestration and setup tasks, rather than
to perform the actual computations.
As shown (see Figure 5), the use of both GPU architectures
(i.e. NVIDIA and AMD) provides extra performance concern-
ing the use of just the AMD GPU, providing acceleration
above 1.5× and about 2× for AXPY and DOT computations
respectively.
4
Conclusions
SEER capabilities were extended to leverage extreme het-
erogeneity to operate on different kinds of accelerators co-
existing in the same computational domain. The test cases
based on the well-known CG algorithm were performed on
the extremely heterogeneous ORNL’s ExCL Zenith (AMD
+ NVIDIA) system. We reported speedups of about 1.5× by
using the new SEER capabilities. This affirms SEER as a valu-
able tool for researchers and developers seeking to optimize
performance across diverse hardware architectures.

Artifact Description for Reproducibility
The test case based on the Conjugate Gradient algorithm and
can be found in the following repository: https://code.ornl.
gov/jhonnygzz1357/seer-jhonnygzz-1357.git. The working
directory is in the next path: /seer-jhonnygzz-1357/tests/test-
CG. Within this directory, you can find different files. The
test.cpp file uses SEER-node to exploit heterogeneous archi-
tectures. The Makefile is used as a template to compile the dif-
ferent files and link them together. Edit the Makefile to your
hardware specifications. The Makefile requires the paths for
the compilers and various flags that will have to be set as
well. Once the Makefile is set up, compile the CG test case
by going to the test-CG directory under tests/test-CG. The
graphs found in the paper were made from these findings.
After changing the sizes, make sure to compile the test case.
To do so, type make in the file directory and the Makefile
will automatically compile it. If recompiling, type make clean
followed by make. This will create an executable run that
will print the runtime for each function execution. The CG
test case will take less than 10 seconds to execute and will
provide the time taken to perform parallel_for and paral-
lel_reduce for AXPY and DOT operations. For our analysis,
the tests were run multiple times with different sizes. For
the sake of clarity, Figure 6 illustrates a pseudocode with the
main components of the CG algorithm implemented using
SEER_node.
